advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Confirm `drain`'s cap-based routing is the intended contract, or key routing on ORDER-BY/exhaustiveness rather than presence of a cap.
evidence: docstring asserts 'A CAPPED query is the ORDER BY updated DESC top-N read' — an assumption about the ONLY capped caller, not enforced
Only two callers exist today (fetcher.py:549-551): active(cap=None) and done(cap=_DONE_RECENT_CAP), so no current bug, but the coupling is implicit.
advisory.finding: `drain` decides partition-vs-single-query solely on `cap is None`, conflating 'exhaustive' with 'uncapped'. A future/other caller passing a non-None `cap` on a non-ORDER-BY exhaustive query would silently skip partitioning and remain exposed to the very ceiling this change removes, with no error distinguishing that path from the intended top-N done-query path.
scenarios: A new caller adds a bounded-but-exhaustive query with a client-side cap and unknowingly bypasses the partitioner.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Confirm the per-pass ACLI call growth under partitioning is acceptable against Jira rate limits and pass-time budget.
evidence: src/rebar/_engine/rebar_reconciler/fetch_paging.py:356: `while pending:` with children pushed on every ceiling hit
Ticket implementation comment: 'the drain settles at roughly six windows, four of which are ceiling probes — about 100 ACLI calls where today's query makes 14.'
_MAX_SPAN=timedelta(days=365*40) bounds only the unbounded-edge walk, not total windows.
advisory.finding: `collect_partitioned` can issue a very large number of ACLI calls for a window-blind or pathologically dense working set (the ticket notes ~100 calls at REB's size, and forward/backward walks add empty probes up to _MAX_SPAN=40yr / _INITIAL_SPAN=30d ≈ log2(40yr/30d)≈9 levels each edge). There is no aggregate call budget across the whole drain — only per-edge span/minute guards — so cost scales with the number of ceiling-hitting windows and is unbounded by any single limit.
scenarios: A project whose active set is a large multiple of the ceiling produces many bisection levels, each a live ACLI round-trip against Jira.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Avoid re-fetching pages already read: raise the ceiling earlier (before draining a full window) or reuse/skip already-drained pages so partitioned drain cost stays ~O(N) rather than O(N × subdivision depth).
evidence: fetch_paging.py:359 `issues.extend(collect(client, _window_jql(jql, lo, hi), page_size=page_size))` — a fresh full paged drain per window

fetch_paging.py:147-152 the ceiling raise fires only AFTER ~1199 issues (~12 pages) have already been fetched from the network for that window, and those pages are dropped when the SilentTruncationError unwinds
fetch_paging.py:366-371 on ceiling the window is split into two sub-windows that re-issue collect() over the same created range from start_at=0, re-fetching the pages the parent just read
fetch_paging.py:353-355 the root window is `(None, None)`, so the FIRST drain always attempts the entire project up to the ceiling before any split — the largest possible discarded read
advisory.finding: On every ACLI ceiling hit, collect_partitioned re-drains work already fetched: collect() pages a window from start_at=0 up to ~_ACLI_CEILING issues (≈12 remote search_issues calls) BEFORE raising, and those pages are discarded; the two sub-windows then re-fetch the same created range. Because each level of subdivision re-fetches the issues already read by its parent, total remote page-fetches scale as O(N × depth) with depth ≈ log2(N/_ACLI_CEILING) plus walk-back probes, rather than O(N) — the round-trip cost degrades super-linearly as the project working set grows, which is the very scale the change exists to handle.
scenarios: A project working set materially above _ACLI_CEILING (e.g. the measured REB 4,380 / 5,000-issue tests) drained against live Jira: each of the log-depth levels re-issues ~12 page calls per overflowing window, so a 5,000-issue drain issues many multiples of the 50 pages a linear scan needs.
Deep subdivision (working set several multiples of the ceiling) multiplies the discarded-then-refetched pages at every level.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Bound or short-circuit walk-back probes so an over-ceiling unbounded edge does not trigger repeated full-ceiling drains that are discarded.
evidence: fetch_paging.py:320-327 walk-back returns a new bounded edge (`hi - span` / `lo + span`) that is re-drained by collect() from scratch
fetch_paging.py:359 each pending window (including every walk-back probe) is drained by a fresh full collect() up to the ceiling before it may raise again
test file _FORWARD_WALK_BUDGET=25 and comment `measured: 11 with the span ceiling, 16 without` — confirms multiple over-large probe drains occur on future-heavy sets
advisory.finding: For a window unbounded on one edge (the root and any [lo, None) / [None, hi) window over the ceiling), _split_window walks the open edge geometrically (span, 2*span, ...) and each probe re-issues a full collect() drain of a still-over-large window from start_at=0 before it can be judged over-ceiling — so a working set skewed toward recent/future created dates (e.g. many issues created after _now()) pays repeated full-ceiling-sized drains per walk-back probe rather than one.
scenarios: A future-heavy or recent-heavy working set where the [now, None) window itself exceeds the ceiling: the forward walk issues several full-ceiling drains (up to _FORWARD_WALK_BUDGET windows) that are each discarded on the ceiling hit before narrowing succeeds.
